stem: A 63-year-old man on simvastatin for high cholesterol has a second lipid drug added because his triglycerides are high. Ten days later he has severe aching in his thighs, weakness and dark brown urine. Creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L and creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. The urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells.
oneliner: 63M + simvastatin + 2nd lipid drug for high TG + 10 d later muscle pain, weakness, brown urine + CK 48,000 + Cr 3.1 + dipstick blood, no RBCs → which drug was added?
ask: Which drug was most likely added?

whyNot.A: Blocks **cholesterol absorption in the gut**; rarely adds to muscle injury
whyNot.B: **Bile acid binder**; raises triglycerides, not used for them
whyNot.E: **Bile acid binder**; stays in the gut

why: **Triglyceride drug + statin → severe muscle pain, very high CK, brown urine with blood on dipstick but no red cells** = rhabdomyolysis. **Gemfibrozil** raises statin levels and adds its own muscle toxicity.

drug.name: Gemfibrozil
drug.how: Activates PPAR-alpha → more lipoprotein lipase → triglycerides fall
drug.watch: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis with statins, gallstones

stem: A 57-year-old woman started an ACE inhibitor for hypertension 6 weeks ago. Over the past week she has had two sudden episodes of swelling that each took about 2 days to settle, and this morning her voice sounds muffled. She has no hives, itching or wheezing, and no family history of recurrent swelling.
oneliner: 57F + ACE inhibitor started 6 wk ago + 2 sudden swelling episodes, muffled voice + no hives, itching or wheeze + no family history → which mediator?
ask: Accumulation of which substance most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.A: **Histamine** swelling comes with hives and itch and settles within hours; none here
whyNot.C: **Leukotrienes** drive wheeze and bronchoconstriction; no wheeze here
whyNot.D: **PAF** acts in anaphylaxis with hives and low blood pressure; absent here
whyNot.E: **Falls** when ACE is blocked, so it cannot be the cause

why: **Non-itchy swelling weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor** = angioedema. ACE normally degrades **bradykinin**; blocking it lets bradykinin build up and leak fluid from vessels.

drug.name: Lisinopril / enalapril
drug.how: Blocks ACE (kininase II): less angiotensin II, more bradykinin
drug.use: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy
drug.watch: Angioedema (any time), dry cough, hyperkalemia, fetal toxicity, creatinine rise in renal artery stenosis

image.prompt: Close-up photograph of a woman's face with marked swelling of the lips and lower face and a slightly enlarged tongue, skin otherwise normal with no hives.

stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension has had a dry, tickling cough for 2 months that is worse at night. He has no fever, sputum, wheeze or heartburn, and he has never smoked. A chest radiograph is normal. A second blood pressure drug was added to his thiazide 3 months ago.
oneliner: 61M + hypertension + 2 mo dry tickling cough + no fever, sputum, wheeze + normal CXR + 2nd BP drug added 3 mo ago → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused the cough?

whyNot.A: **ARB**: does not block ACE, so no bradykinin build-up; cough is not a feature
whyNot.B: **Alpha-1 blocker**: first-dose orthostatic hypotension, not cough
whyNot.C: **Beta-blocker**: can cause bronchospasm, but he has **no wheeze**
whyNot.E: **Calcium channel blocker**: constipation, flushing, edema; not a cough

why: **Dry, non-productive cough with a normal chest film after adding a BP drug** = ACE inhibitor cough. Blocked ACE lets **bradykinin and substance P** accumulate in the airway.

drug.name: Enalapril
drug.how: Blocks ACE (kininase II): bradykinin and substance P build up
drug.watch: Dry cough (stop drug, switch to ARB), angioedema, hyperkalemia, teratogenic

stem: A newborn boy has no urine output for the first 36 hours, a flattened face, and poorly expanded lungs on chest radiograph. Skull films show widely open sutures with poor ossification of the calvarium. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios in the second trimester. The mother took one antihypertensive drug throughout pregnancy.
oneliner: Newborn boy + anuria for 36 h + flat face, hypoplastic lungs + poorly ossified skull + mother had oligohydramnios + took one antihypertensive → which drug?
ask: Which drug did the mother most likely take?

whyNot.A: **Beta/alpha-blocker**: considered safe in pregnancy; does not cause fetal renal failure
whyNot.B: **Central alpha-2 agonist**: a preferred pregnancy drug
whyNot.C: **Calcium channel blocker**: acceptable in pregnancy, no fetal renal syndrome
whyNot.D: **Direct vasodilator**: acceptable in pregnancy, no fetal renal syndrome

why: **Oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia and poor skull ossification** = ACE inhibitor fetopathy. Angiotensin II is needed for fetal glomerular filtration, so the fetus makes little urine and amniotic fluid.

drug.name: Lisinopril
drug.how: Blocks angiotensin II formation; fetal GFR falls
drug.watch: Contraindicated in pregnancy (renal failure, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia); switch to labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine or hydralazine

stem: A 74-year-old woman has had shortness of breath on climbing one flight of stairs for the past 2 weeks. Her lungs are clear and she has no leg swelling. Her pupils are normal in size and she has no excess salivation or sweating. Spirometry shows an FEV1 that is 25% lower than last year. Two weeks ago her ophthalmologist started eyedrops for glaucoma.
oneliner: 74F + 2 wk exertional dyspnea + clear lungs, no edema + normal pupils, no drooling or sweating + FEV1 down 25% + glaucoma drops 2 wk ago → which drug?
ask: Which of the following eyedrops most likely caused her symptoms?

whyNot.A: **Alpha-2 agonist**: causes dry mouth and fatigue, not bronchospasm
whyNot.B: **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor**: stinging and bitter taste
whyNot.C: **Prostaglandin analog**: eyelash growth and iris darkening
whyNot.E: **Cholinesterase inhibitor**: would give small pupils, drooling and sweating; **absent**

why: **New dyspnea and lower FEV1 after starting glaucoma drops, with no cholinergic signs** = beta-blocker eyedrops. Timolol is absorbed through the nasolacrimal duct, and **beta-2 blockade** narrows the airways.

drug.name: Timolol (topical)
drug.how: Blocks ciliary beta receptors: less aqueous humor production

stem: A 62-year-old man with stable angina is started on a long-acting oral drug that lowers cardiac preload by dilating veins and raises coronary flow.
oneliner: 62M + stable angina + new long-acting drug that lowers preload by venodilation → most common adverse effect?
ask: Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of this drug?

whyNot.A: Typical of **beta-blockers and verapamil**, not a venodilator
whyNot.C: Typical of **loop diuretics**, not a venodilator
whyNot.D: Typical of **digoxin toxicity**, not a venodilator

why: **A preload-lowering venodilator for angina** = an organic nitrate. NO-driven vasodilation reaches **cerebral vessels**, giving throbbing headache, flushing and sometimes orthostasis.

drug.name: Isosorbide mononitrate / nitroglycerin
drug.how: Releases NO: cGMP up, vein dilation
drug.watch: Headache, flushing, orthostatic hypotension, tolerance; never with PDE5 inhibitors

stem: A 58-year-old man takes isosorbide dinitrate for angina. One hour after taking a tablet from a friend for erectile dysfunction, he faints at home. Blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg and pulse is 108/min. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a normal PR interval and a normal QT interval. He has no chest pain.
oneliner: 58M + isosorbide dinitrate + friend's erectile dysfunction tablet 1 h earlier + syncope + BP 60/30, HR 108 + ECG sinus tachycardia, normal PR and QT → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains his hypotension?

options.B: Torsades de pointes from QT prolongation
options.D: More cGMP made by nitrate-derived NO, with less cGMP broken down

whyNot.A: The **PR interval is normal** and the rate is fast, not slow
whyNot.B: The **QT is normal** and the rhythm is sinus
whyNot.C: The rate is **fast (108/min)**, which does not fit beta-blockade
whyNot.E: No hives, wheeze or itch; the timing fits a **drug interaction**, not allergy

why: **Nitrate + erectile dysfunction tablet → syncope with profound hypotension** = PDE5 inhibitor plus NO donor. The nitrate raises **cGMP production**, the PDE5 inhibitor stops **cGMP breakdown**, so vasodilation is exaggerated.

drug.name: Sildenafil
drug.how: Blocks cGMP breakdown, prolonging NO-driven vasodilation
drug.watch: Severe hypotension with nitrates, blue-tinted vision, flushing, headache

stem: A 49-year-old man with a blood pressure of 230/130 mm Hg and papilledema is given a continuous intravenous vasodilator infusion at a high rate for 48 hours. His blood pressure is now 150/90 mm Hg, but he is lethargic and breathing rapidly. Arterial pH is 7.21, serum bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, lactate 9 mmol/L and PaO2 is normal. His kidney function is normal.
oneliner: 49M + hypertensive emergency + IV vasodilator infusion at high rate for 48 h + now lethargic, rapid breathing + pH 7.21, HCO3 12, lactate 9, normal PaO2 → which substance?
ask: Accumulation of which of the following most likely explains this picture?

whyNot.A: The **intended active molecule**; it acts for seconds and does not cause lactic acidosis
whyNot.C: The drug contains iron, but it is **not released in toxic amounts**

why: **Prolonged high-rate nitroprusside + lactic acidosis, lethargy and normal PaO2** = cyanide toxicity. Cyanide blocks **cytochrome c oxidase**, so cells go anaerobic. Treat with **hydroxocobalamin** (or nitrite + thiosulfate).

drug.name: Sodium nitroprusside
drug.how: Releases NO: cGMP up, arteries and veins dilate
drug.watch: Cyanide toxicity (lactic acidosis), thiocyanate toxicity in renal failure, hypotension

stem: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had aching in both thighs and shoulders and difficulty rising from chairs for 1 week. His urine is dark brown. Creatine kinase is 11,200 U/L and creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. His medications are metformin, captopril, verapamil, rosiglitazone and pravastatin. Pravastatin was started 2 months ago; the others were taken for years.
oneliner: 57M + diabetes + 1 wk thigh and shoulder aching, weakness + dark urine + CK 11,200 + meds metformin, captopril, verapamil, rosiglitazone, pravastatin (new 2 mo ago) → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused his muscle symptoms?

whyNot.A: Causes **GI upset and lactic acidosis**, not muscle injury; taken for years
whyNot.B: **ACE inhibitor**: cough and angioedema; taken for years
whyNot.C: **Calcium channel blocker**: constipation and edema; taken for years
whyNot.D: **Thiazolidinedione**: fluid retention and weight gain; taken for years

why: **New statin followed by proximal myalgia, weakness, very high CK and dark urine** = statin myopathy progressing to rhabdomyolysis. Statins can injure muscle; stop the drug and give fluids.

drug.name: Pravastatin
drug.how: Blocks cholesterol synthesis; raises hepatic LDL receptors
drug.watch: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, transaminase rise; risk rises with fibrates, niacin, CYP3A4 inhibitors

stem: A 66-year-old man takes simvastatin. A second lipid-lowering drug was added 3 weeks ago. He now has severe muscle pain and weakness and passes dark brown urine. Creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL and creatine kinase is 52,000 U/L. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows only 0-1 red cells per high-power field and no red cell casts.
oneliner: 66M + simvastatin + 2nd lipid drug added 3 wk ago + severe muscle pain, dark urine + Cr 1.0 → 3.4, CK 52,000 + dipstick blood but 0-1 RBC, no casts → which pigment?
ask: The dipstick-positive, red-cell-negative urine is most likely due to which of the following?

whyNot.A: Hemolysis would drop haptoglobin and give a **normal CK**
whyNot.B: Glomerulonephritis shows **dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts**; none present
whyNot.C: Obstruction gives **pale stools and conjugated bilirubin**; no such features, and CK is not explained
whyNot.E: CK of 52,000 and muscle pain point to **muscle breakdown**, not crystals

why: **Statin plus a new lipid drug, severe myalgia, CK 52,000, heme-positive urine with no red cells** = rhabdomyolysis. **Gemfibrozil** raises statin levels; **myoglobin** turns urine dipstick positive and injures the tubules.

drug.name: Gemfibrozil
drug.how: PPAR-alpha agonist: more lipoprotein lipase, lower VLDL; also slows statin glucuronidation
drug.watch: Myopathy with statins, gallstones, GI upset

stem: A 33-year-old woman began a new nutritional supplement 20 minutes ago and now feels warm and itchy over her face, neck and upper chest. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse is 84/min. She has no wheeze, no voice change, no abdominal pain, and her lips and tongue are not swollen.
oneliner: 33F + new supplement 20 min ago + warm, itchy face, neck, chest + BP 118/72, HR 84 + no wheeze, voice change, or lip swelling → which supplement?
ask: Which of the following supplements most likely caused this?

whyNot.A: Excess causes **GI upset and kidney stones**, not flushing
whyNot.B: Excess is **benign** and may mask B12 deficiency

why: **Warmth, itch and skin redness soon after a new supplement, without airway or blood-pressure involvement** = niacin flush, from **prostaglandin D2** acting on skin vessels. Aspirin taken beforehand reduces it.

drug.name: Niacin
drug.how: Activates GPR109A: PGD2 release causes cutaneous vasodilation
drug.watch: Flushing and itch, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hepatotoxicity

image.prompt: Photograph of a young woman whose face, neck and upper chest show diffuse bright red flushing, with no swelling of the lips or tongue.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in after swallowing tablets from his grandfather's pillbox, which holds either aspirin or dicumarol. He has scattered bruises and gum bleeding. His platelet count is 280,000/mm3. The grandfather cannot say which drug the tablets were.
oneliner: 4M + swallowed tablets from grandfather's pillbox (aspirin or dicumarol) + bruises, gum bleeding + platelets 280,000 → which lab result favors dicumarol?
ask: Which of the following findings would indicate dicumarol rather than aspirin?

options.B: Prolonged bleeding time with normal prothrombin time

whyNot.A: Platelet count is already **normal** at 280,000; neither drug causes thrombocytopenia
whyNot.B: This is the **aspirin** pattern: platelet dysfunction, normal clotting factors
whyNot.C: Neither drug lowers **fibrinogen**; DIC is not suggested
whyNot.D: Coumarins **prolong** PTT slightly, never shorten it

answer: Prolonged PT (dicumarol, like warfarin, lowers factors II, VII, IX, X)
why: **Both drugs cause bruising, but only a coumarin lowers clotting factors.** Dicumarol blocks vitamin K recycling, so **PT is prolonged** (factor VII has the shortest half-life); aspirin leaves PT normal.

drug.name: Dicumarol
drug.how: Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase: II, VII, IX, X not carboxylated
drug.use: Historical oral anticoagulant (same class as warfarin)
drug.watch: Bleeding with prolonged PT/INR; reversed by vitamin K

stem: A 58-year-old woman is admitted with a pulmonary embolism and given a continuous intravenous anticoagulant infusion titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time. Her platelet count on admission was 160,000/mm3. On day 7 her platelets are 55,000/mm3, and she has a new swollen, painful left calf. There is no bleeding and she has no history of liver disease.
oneliner: 58F + pulmonary embolism + IV anticoagulant infusion titrated to aPTT + platelets 160,000 → 55,000 on day 7 + new swollen painful calf + no bleeding → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused the fall in platelets?

whyNot.A: Given by mouth and monitored with **INR**, not aPTT
whyNot.C: A thrombolytic: causes **bleeding**, not a fall in platelets with new clots
whyNot.D: Taken orally; **does not cause** immune thrombocytopenia
whyNot.E: Oral factor Xa inhibitor, **not titrated to aPTT**

why: **Falling platelets about 5-10 days into an aPTT-titrated infusion, with a NEW clot** = heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. **Antibodies to heparin-PF4 complexes** activate platelets, so platelets fall and clots form. Stop heparin and give a direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban).

drug.name: Heparin
drug.how: Activates antithrombin III: inactivates thrombin and factor Xa
drug.watch: HIT (antibodies to PF4-heparin), bleeding (protamine reverses), osteoporosis

stem: A 70-year-old man has taken warfarin for 10 years with a stable INR of 2.4. Two weeks ago he started a new over-the-counter drug for heartburn. He now has gum bleeding and large bruises on his arms. His INR is 6.1. He has had no change in diet, alcohol intake, or other drugs.
oneliner: 70M + warfarin 10 y, INR stable at 2.4 + new heartburn drug 2 wk ago + gum bleeding, bruises + INR 6.1 + no change in diet, alcohol, other drugs → which drug?
ask: Which of the following new drugs most likely explains this change?

whyNot.A: **H2 blocker without CYP inhibition**; does not change warfarin metabolism
whyNot.B: Binds in the gut; if anything **lowers** absorption, which would lower INR
whyNot.E: Prokinetic; **no CYP effect**, not an acid reducer

why: **A stable warfarin patient develops a high INR soon after adding a heartburn drug** = CYP450 inhibition. **Cimetidine** inhibits several CYP enzymes, so warfarin clearance falls and INR rises.

drug.name: Cimetidine
drug.how: Blocks gastric H2 receptors; inhibits CYP450 enzymes
drug.watch: CYP inhibition (warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin), gynecomastia, confusion in the elderly

stem: A 66-year-old man with atrial fibrillation was started on an antiarrhythmic drug 8 months ago and has stayed in sinus rhythm. He now has fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and a 4-kg weight gain. TSH is 21 mIU/L with a low free T4. He has no history of thyroid disease, and his cough, liver tests and chest radiograph are normal.
oneliner: 66M + atrial fibrillation + antiarrhythmic started 8 mo ago, in sinus rhythm + fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain + TSH 21, low free T4 + no thyroid history → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.A: **Cardiac glycoside**: visual and GI toxicity; **no thyroid effect**
whyNot.D: Causes **proarrhythmia** in structural heart disease; no thyroid effect
whyNot.E: Causes **cinchonism** (tinnitus, headache) and QT prolongation; no thyroid effect

answer: Amiodarone (hypothyroidism from iodine load and Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
why: **Months after starting an AF antiarrhythmic, hypothyroid symptoms with high TSH** = amiodarone. It is **iodine-rich** and structurally like thyroid hormone, so it can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism.

drug.name: Amiodarone
drug.class: Class III antiarrhythmic (also I, II, IV effects)
drug.how: Blocks K+ channels (and Na+, Ca2+, beta): prolongs action potential and QT
drug.watch: Hypo/hyperthyroidism, pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits, blue-gray skin, QT prolongation

stem: A 57-year-old man with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and symptomatic premature ventricular beats is started on a twice-daily antiarrhythmic. His pulse falls from 78 to 64/min. ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QRS duration of 90 ms and a corrected QT interval of 520 ms, which was 430 ms before treatment.
oneliner: 57M + paroxysmal AF and PVCs + new twice-daily antiarrhythmic + pulse 78 → 64 + QRS 90 ms + QTc 430 → 520 ms → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.A: Widens the **QRS** (sodium channel block); QRS here is normal
whyNot.B: Slows the rate but **does not lengthen the QT**
whyNot.C: Given IV with a half-life of **seconds**; not a twice-daily drug
whyNot.D: Pure K+ channel blocker: prolongs QT but **does not slow the heart rate**

why: **Slower pulse plus a longer QT on an AF/PVC drug** = sotalol. It has **beta-blocking** action (slows the rate) and **class III K+ channel blockade** (prolongs QT, risk of torsades).

drug.name: Sotalol
drug.class: Class III antiarrhythmic with beta-blocking action
drug.how: Blocks K+ channels (prolongs repolarization) and beta receptors
drug.watch: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, bradycardia, bronchospasm, fatigue

stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure has nausea, confusion and yellow-tinted vision for 2 days. He takes digoxin, furosemide and carvedilol. Serum digoxin is 4.8 ng/mL, potassium is 7.2 mEq/L, and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. The blood sample was not hemolyzed, creatine kinase is normal, and he takes no ACE inhibitor, potassium-sparing diuretic or potassium supplement.
oneliner: 74M + heart failure on digoxin, furosemide, carvedilol + nausea, confusion, yellow vision + digoxin 4.8 + K 7.2 + Cr 1.1 + no hemolysis, normal CK, no ACEi or K supplement → why high K?
ask: Which of the following best explains the hyperkalemia?

options.B: Increased potassium reabsorption in the collecting duct
options.C: In vitro hemolysis of the blood sample
options.D: Inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase, so cells take up less potassium
options.E: Release of potassium from injured muscle cells

whyNot.A: Needs diabetes or renal disease; he has **normal creatinine** and no related drugs
whyNot.B: Not expected with **furosemide** (which increases potassium loss) and normal creatinine
whyNot.E: **CK is normal**, so muscle is not injured

answer: Na+/K+ ATPase inhibition → potassium stays outside cells
why: **Digoxin toxicity with high potassium** = pump poisoning. Digoxin blocks the **Na+/K+ ATPase**, so potassium cannot enter cells and serum K rises. High K in digoxin overdose predicts worse outcome; treat with **digoxin Fab fragments**.

drug.name: Digoxin
drug.how: Blocks Na+/K+ ATPase: Na+ in, Ca2+ up via Na/Ca exchange, more contractility, vagal tone up
drug.watch: Nausea, confusion, yellow-green vision, arrhythmias, hyperkalemia in overdose; antidote digoxin Fab

stem: A 33-year-old man with allergic rhinitis has used oxymetazoline nasal spray every day for 3 weeks. His congestion is now worse and returns soon after each dose wears off.
oneliner: 33M + allergic rhinitis + oxymetazoline spray daily for 3 weeks + congestion worse as each dose wears off → adverse effect?
ask: Which adverse effect best explains his worsening symptoms?

whyNot.A: Would give **raised blood pressure**, not congestion that returns as each dose wears off
whyNot.C: Would give **crusting and bleeding**, not swelling that recurs between doses
whyNot.D: Loss of smell, not a **cycle of congestion** tied to the dose
whyNot.E: An alpha-1 effect on the **bladder neck**; it does not explain worse nasal congestion

answer: Rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) from prolonged topical alpha-agonist use
why: Topical **alpha-agonist decongestants** used for **more than a few days** cause **rebound congestion**: the mucosa becomes dependent and swells when each dose wears off. **Oral** decongestants (pseudoephedrine) instead risk raised blood pressure.

idea.rule: Short courses only: topical alpha-agonist sprays for 3 days or less, then stop.
also: Oral pseudoephedrine can raise blood pressure and heart rate
Phenylephrine (alpha-1) and oxymetazoline (alpha-1 and alpha-2) are both vasoconstrictors
Treatment is stopping the spray and using a nasal steroid
Cocaine nasal damage differs: septal necrosis

drug.name: Oxymetazoline
drug.use: Short-term nasal congestion (no more than 3 days)
drug.watch: Rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) with longer use
